name: Question 7
problem:
$$
{y}^{″}-2{y}^{′}-15y=-7{e}^{4x}
$$

Consider the differential equation above, for which the corresponding complementary solution is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{5x}+B{e}^{-3x},$ where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants. Select the correct options below.$\,$
The function ${y}_{p}(x)={e}^{4x}$ 
{{field-1}} 
a particular solution of the differential equation.

$\,$
The function ${y}_{p}(x)=x{e}^{4x}$ 
{{field-2}} 
a particular solution of the differential equation.

$\,$
The general solution of the differential equation is given by

$\,\,$
$y(x)=$ 
{{field-3}}
$+$
{{field-4}},

$\,$
where 
{{field-5}} are arbitrary constants.
worked_solution:
For an inhomogeneous differential equation, the general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

where

- ${y}_{c}(x)$ is the complementary solution (the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous equation), and

- ${y}_{p}(x)$ is a particular solution of the original inhomogeneous equation.

With this in mind, let's check which of the two given functions is a particular solution of our inhomogeneous equation:

- For ${y}_{p}(x)={e}^{4x},$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =({e}^{4x})^{′}=4{e}^{4x}, \\ {y}^{″}(x) & =(4{e}^{4x})^{′}=16{e}^{4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the equation, we have

$$
(16{e}^{4x})-2(4{e}^{4x})-15({e}^{4x})=-7{e}^{4x}.\,\,✓
$$

So, ${y}_{p}(x)={e}^{4x}$ $\text{is}$ a particular solution of the differential equation.

- For ${y}_{p}(x)=x{e}^{4x},$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =(x{e}^{4x})^{′}={e}^{4x}+4x{e}^{4x}, \\ {y}^{″}(x) & =({e}^{4x}+4x{e}^{4x})^{′}=8{e}^{4x}+16x{e}^{4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the equation, we have

$$
(8{e}^{4x}+16x{e}^{4x})-2({e}^{4x}+4x{e}^{4x})-15(x{e}^{4x})=-7{e}^{4x}.\,\,\times 
$$

So, ${y}_{p}(x)=x{e}^{4x}$ $\text{isn't}$ a particular solution of the differential equation.

We are told that the complementary solution of our equation is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{5x}+B{e}^{-3x}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & ={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x) \\  & =A{e}^{5x}+B{e}^{-3x}+{e}^{4x}\end{aligned}
$$

where $A\text{ and }B$ are arbitrary constants.

EXPLANATION

For an inhomogeneous differential equation, the general solution is given by y(x)=yc(x)+yp(x), where

  • yc(x) is the complementary solution (the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous equation), and

  • yp(x) is a particular solution of the original inhomogeneous equation.

With this in mind, let's check which of the two given functions is a particular solution of our inhomogeneous equation:

  • For yp(x)=e4x, we have y′(x)=(e4x)′=4e4x,y″(x)=(4e4x)′=16e4x. Substituting this into the equation, we have (16e4x)−2(4e4x)−15(e4x)=−7e4x.✓ So, yp(x)=e4x is a particular solution of the differential equation.

  • For yp(x)=xe4x, we have y′(x)=(xe4x)′=e4x+4xe4x,y″(x)=(e4x+4xe4x)′=8e4x+16xe4x. Substituting this into the equation, we have (8e4x+16xe4x)−2(e4x+4xe4x)−15(xe4x)=−7e4x.× So, yp(x)=xe4x isn't a particular solution of the differential equation.

We are told that the complementary solution of our equation is yc(x)=Ae5x+Be−3x. Therefore, the general solution is y(x)=yc(x)+yp(x)=Ae5x+Be−3x+e4x where A and B are arbitrary constants.
